at klare sig.explanation: "At klare sig" means "to get by / do well". To say someone is doing well in a place, say: "Hun klarer sig fint i Danmark" (She is doing fine in Denmark). To say you manage without something, add "uden" (without): "Jeg klarer mig uden bil" (I get by without a car).

at klassificere.explanation: "At klassificere" means "to classify". It comes from "en klasse" (a class).

at klatre.explanation: "At klatre" means "to climb", as in going up with hands and feet. To say children climb a tree, say: "Børnene klatrer i et træ" (The children climb a tree). To say prices go up, use the same verb: "Priserne klatrer" (Prices are climbing).

at klemme.explanation: "At klemme" means "to squeeze / pinch". To say your finger got caught in a door, say: "Jeg klemte fingeren i døren" (I pinched my finger in the door).

at klikke.explanation: "At klikke" means "to click". To name the item you click, add "på" (on) before the item: "Jeg klikker på linket" (I click on the link). To click twice quickly, use "at dobbeltklikke" (to double-click): "Dobbeltklik på ikonet" (Double-click the icon).

at klippe.explanation: "At klippe" means "to cut (with scissors)". To cut paper with scissors, say: "Jeg klipper papir" (I cut paper). To say a hairdresser cuts hair, use the same verb: "Hun klipper mit hår" (She cuts my hair).

at klynge sig.explanation: "At klynge sig" means "to cling". To say what you cling to, add "til" (to): "Han klynger sig til rækværket" (He clings to the railing). The same pattern works for feelings: "Hun klynger sig til håbet" (She clings to hope).

at klæde.explanation: "At klæde" means "to suit". To say a color or clothes look good on someone, put the person after the verb: "Blåt klæder hende" (Blue suits her). With "sig" (oneself) it means dressing yourself: "Jeg klæder mig på" (I get dressed).

at klæde sig af.explanation: "At klæde sig af" means "to get undressed". The small word after "klæde" changes with the person: "Jeg klæder mig af" (I get undressed), "Hun klæder sig af" (She gets undressed). The opposite is "at klæde sig på" (to get dressed): "Jeg klæder mig på" (I get dressed).

at klæde sig på.explanation: "At klæde sig på" means "to get dressed". The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with the person: "Du klæder dig på" (You get dressed), "Han klæder sig på" (He gets dressed). To put on one item, say "at tage en jakke på" (to put on a jacket): "Jeg tager jakken på" (I put on the jacket).

at klø.explanation: "At klø" means "to itch / scratch". To say something itches, say: "Det klør" (It itches). To scratch yourself, add "sig" (oneself): "Jeg klør mig i hovedet" (I scratch my head).

at klø sig.explanation: "At klø sig" means "to scratch oneself". It is built from "at klø" (to itch / scratch) and "sig" (oneself). To name the body part you scratch, add "på" (on) before it: "Jeg klør mig på ryggen" (I scratch my back).

at knappe.explanation: "At knappe" means "to button". To say what you button, name it after the verb: "Han knapper skjorten" (He buttons the shirt). To open the buttons again, add "op" (up): "Jeg knapper jakken op" (I unbutton the jacket).

at knibe.explanation: "At knibe" means "to pinch / squint". To say someone pinched you, say: "Hun kneb mig i armen" (She pinched my arm). To say someone squints, add "øjnene sammen" (the eyes together): "Han kniber øjnene sammen" (He squints). When money is short, say: "Det kniber med pengene" (Money is tight).

at knuse.explanation: "At knuse" means "to crush". To say something broke into pieces, like glass, say: "Han knuste glasset" (He smashed the glass). It also works for feelings: "Det knuste hendes hjerte" (It broke her heart).

at knytte.explanation: "At knytte" means "to tie / connect". To clench a fist, say: "Han knytter næven" (He clenches his fist). To form a friendship, say: "De knytter et venskab" (They form a friendship). For tying shoelaces, use "at binde" (to tie): "Jeg binder mine snørebånd" (I tie my shoelaces).

at knække.explanation: "At knække" means "to crack / break". To say you break a stick, say: "Jeg knækker en pind" (I break a stick). For a broken bone, use "at brække" (to break): "Jeg har brækket armen" (I have broken my arm).

at knæle.explanation: "At knæle" means "to kneel". It comes from "et knæ" (a knee). To say someone proposed on one knee, say: "Han knælede og friede" (He knelt and proposed).

at koge.explanation: "At koge" means "to boil". To say water is bubbling hot, say: "Vandet koger" (The water is boiling). To boil food in water, name the food: "Jeg koger æg" (I boil eggs). For making a meal, use "at lave mad" (to cook): "Jeg laver mad" (I am cooking).

at koge over.explanation: "At koge over" means "to boil over". To say milk runs out of the pot, say: "Mælken koger over" (The milk boils over). It also works for feelings: "Hun koger over af vrede" (She is boiling over with anger).

at kollidere.explanation: "At kollidere" means "to collide". To name what you hit, add "med" (with): "Bilen kolliderede med en cykel" (The car collided with a bicycle). When two plans clash, use the same verb: "Mødet kolliderer med min tandlægetid" (The meeting clashes with my dentist appointment).

at kombinere.explanation: "At kombinere" means "to combine". To say which things you put together, join them with "med" (with): "Du kan kombinere en rød trøje med sorte bukser" (You can combine a red sweater with black trousers).

at komme.explanation: "At komme" means "to come". To say you are on your way, say: "Jeg kommer nu" (I am coming now). To ask where someone is from, use it with "fra" (from): "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?). To say what will happen next, use "kommer til at": "Det kommer til at regne" (It is going to rain).

at komme an på.explanation: "At komme an på" means "to depend on". To answer a yes-or-no question when it is not clear, say: "Kommer du?" "Det kommer an på" (Are you coming? It depends). To name what it depends on, add it after "på" (on): "Det kommer an på prisen" (It depends on the price).

at komme for sent.explanation: "At komme for sent" means "to be late". Literally, it is "to come too late". To say you were late, say: "Jeg kom for sent til skolen" (I was late for school). For a train or bus, use "forsinket" (delayed): "Toget er forsinket" (The train is delayed).
